subject: Biology
title: Transport and Support Systems
outline: Explain the need for transport systems and compare materials transported in plants and animals
Describe absorption of water, transpiration, root pressure and translocation
Describe the composition and functions of blood and the mammalian circulatory system
Explain blood groups, clotting and immunity in outline
Compare hydrostatic skeletons, exoskeletons and endoskeletons
Describe the mammalian skeleton, joints, muscles and mechanisms of support in plants

modules.title: Transport in Plants
modules.html:
1. Need for Transport

Unicellular organisms exchange materials directly by diffusion because of their large surface area to volume ratio. Larger, multicellular organisms have a small ratio and greater distances between cells and the environment, so they require specialised transport systems.

2. Absorption and Ascent of Water

Water enters root hairs by osmosis and mineral ions largely by active transport. Water then travels across the cortex through the apoplast (cell walls) and symplast (cytoplasm) pathways to the xylem. Its rise up the stem is explained by:

  1. Transpiration pull – cohesion–tension theory: evaporation from the mesophyll creates tension; cohesive water molecules (hydrogen bonding) are pulled up as a continuous column, adhering to the xylem walls.
  2. Root pressure: active pumping of ions into the xylem lowers water potential and pushes water upward; it causes guttation and bleeding of cut stems.
  3. Capillarity: a minor contribution from the narrow xylem vessels.

3. Transpiration

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial parts, mainly through stomata (about 90 %), with smaller losses through the cuticle and lenticels. It is increased by high temperature, low humidity, wind and bright light (which opens stomata), and reduced by the opposite conditions. It is measured with a potometer.

Importance: cools the plant, drives the ascent of water and mineral salts, and maintains turgidity. Excessive transpiration causes wilting; xerophytes reduce it with sunken stomata, thick cuticles, reduced leaves and succulent tissues.

4. Vascular Tissues and Translocation

FeatureXylemPhloem
CellsVessels, tracheids, fibres (dead, lignified)Sieve tubes and companion cells (living)
TransportsWater and mineral saltsManufactured food (sucrose, amino acids)
DirectionUpward onlyBoth directions (source to sink)
EnergyPassiveActive (mass flow, needs ATP)

Ringing (girdling) experiments — removing a ring of bark — cause swelling above the ring, showing that food is translocated downwards in the phloem while water continues to rise in the xylem.

examples.q: A potometer bubble moved 60 mm in 5 minutes in a tube of internal radius 0.5 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake.
examples.a: Volume \( = \pi r^2 l = 3.142 \times (0.5)^2 \times 60 = 47.1\,\text{mm}^3 \) in 5 minutes, giving a rate of \( 47.1/5 = 9.4\,\text{mm}^3\,\text{min}^{-1} \).

examples.q: Why does a plant wilt on a hot afternoon even when the soil is moist?
examples.a: Transpiration exceeds the rate of water absorption by the roots, so cells lose turgor faster than water can be replaced. The leaves and soft stems become flaccid and droop. In the cooler evening absorption catches up and turgor — and shape — are restored.

modules.title: Transport in Animals: Blood and Circulation
modules.html:
1. Composition of Blood

ComponentDescriptionFunction
Plasma (55 %)Water with proteins, salts, food, hormones, wastesTransport medium, distributes heat
ErythrocytesBiconcave, no nucleus, haemoglobinCarry oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin
LeucocytesNucleated; phagocytes and lymphocytesDefence: engulf germs, produce antibodies
PlateletsCell fragmentsInitiate blood clotting

2. Clotting

Damaged tissue and platelets release thromboplastin, which (with calcium ions and vitamin K) converts prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap cells and form a clot. Clotting prevents blood loss and entry of pathogens. Haemophilia is the inherited inability to clot normally.

3. Blood Groups and Transfusion

GroupAntigenAntibody in plasmaCan receive from
AAanti-BA, O
BBanti-AB, O
ABA and BnoneAll (universal recipient)
Ononeanti-A and anti-BO only (universal donor)

The rhesus factor matters in pregnancy: a rhesus-negative mother carrying a rhesus-positive fetus may form antibodies that attack the red cells of a later rhesus-positive fetus (haemolytic disease of the newborn).

4. The Heart and Circulation

The mammalian heart is a four-chambered double pump. Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium. Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → body → vena cava → right atrium. This double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate and maintains high pressure to the body.

ArteryVeinCapillary
Thick muscular elastic wallThinner wallOne cell thick
Narrow lumen, no valves (except at heart)Wide lumen, valves presentVery narrow lumen
Blood at high pressure, in spurtsLow pressure, smooth flowExchange of materials
Carries blood away from heartCarries blood to the heartLinks arterioles and venules

Lymph is tissue fluid that drains into lymph vessels, filters through lymph nodes and returns to the blood; it carries fats from the intestine and plays a role in immunity.

examples.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right?
examples.a: The left ventricle pumps blood through the aorta to the whole body against high resistance, so it needs more cardiac muscle to generate a high pressure. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs at a much lower pressure.

examples.q: Explain why a person of group O is called a universal donor.
examples.a: Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so they are not agglutinated by anti-A or anti-B antibodies in a recipient's plasma. Their blood can therefore be given, in small volumes, to recipients of any ABO group.

modules.title: Support and Movement
modules.html:
1. Functions of Skeletons

Support, protection of delicate organs, locomotion (levers for muscles), shape and, in vertebrates, manufacture of blood cells and storage of mineral salts.

2. Types of Skeleton

  • Hydrostatic skeleton – fluid under pressure in a closed cavity, e.g. earthworm coelom; circular and longitudinal muscles act antagonistically for movement.
  • Exoskeleton – hard chitinous cuticle outside the body of arthropods; protects and prevents water loss but must be moulted (ecdysis) for growth.
  • Endoskeleton – internal bone and cartilage of vertebrates; grows with the body and allows large size.

3. The Mammalian Skeleton

Axial skeleton: skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum. Appendicular skeleton: pectoral and pelvic girdles with the limb bones.

VertebraDistinguishing feature
Atlas (1st cervical)Ring-like, wide neural canal, no centrum; nodding of head
Axis (2nd cervical)Odontoid process; rotation of head
CervicalVertebrarterial canals, short neural spine
ThoracicLong neural spine, facets for ribs
LumbarLarge centrum, transverse processes for strong muscles
SacralFused, joins pelvic girdle
CaudalSmall, reduced processes

4. Joints and Muscles

  • Immovable (fused): sutures of the skull.
  • Slightly movable: between vertebrae, cushioned by cartilage discs.
  • Freely movable (synovial): ball-and-socket (hip, shoulder — movement in all planes) and hinge (elbow, knee — movement in one plane). Synovial fluid lubricates; ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.

Skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs: contraction of the biceps flexes the arm while the triceps relaxes; the triceps contracts to extend it. Muscles can only pull, never push.

5. Support in Plants

Herbaceous plants rely on turgor pressure and collenchyma; woody plants depend on lignified xylem, sclerenchyma fibres and secondary thickening. Additional support comes from buttress roots, prop roots (maize), stilt roots (mangrove), tendrils and twining stems in climbers.

examples.q: Why must an insect moult in order to grow?
examples.a: Its exoskeleton of chitin is rigid and cannot expand. At intervals the insect secretes enzymes that digest the inner layer, splits and sheds the old cuticle (ecdysis), swells its body with air or water and then hardens a new, larger cuticle.

examples.q: Describe how the arm is straightened after being bent.
examples.a: The triceps (extensor) contracts while the biceps (flexor) relaxes. The triceps tendon pulls the ulna at the elbow hinge joint, and the forearm acts as a lever with the elbow as fulcrum, so the arm extends.

quiz.q: Water is absorbed by root hairs mainly by
quiz.solution: Soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap, so water enters by osmosis.

quiz.q: The theory that best explains the ascent of water in tall trees is
quiz.solution: Transpiration pull with cohesive and adhesive water forces can raise water more than 100 m.
About 90 % of water vapour loss is through stomatal pores.
It follows the movement of an air bubble to estimate water uptake, approximating transpiration.

quiz.q: Manufactured food is transported in the
quiz.solution: Sucrose and amino acids move in living sieve tubes assisted by companion cells.

quiz.q: Xylem vessels are especially suited to conduction because they are
quiz.solution: Dead, hollow lignified tubes offer little resistance and give mechanical support.

quiz.q: Which blood cell lacks a nucleus in mammals?
quiz.solution: The mature red blood cell loses its nucleus, creating more room for haemoglobin.

quiz.q: The soluble protein converted to insoluble threads during clotting is
quiz.solution: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin threads that form the clot mesh.

quiz.q: A person of blood group AB is called a universal recipient because the plasma has
quiz.solution: With no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, donated cells of any ABO group are not agglutinated.

quiz.q: Blood is carried from the lungs to the heart by the
quiz.solution: The pulmonary vein is unusual in carrying oxygenated blood towards the heart.

quiz.q: Valves are present in veins in order to
quiz.solution: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so pocket valves stop it flowing backwards.

quiz.q: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart
quiz.solution: Blood goes heart→lungs→heart→body→heart, keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

quiz.q: The earthworm is supported by a
quiz.solution: Coelomic fluid under pressure works with circular and longitudinal muscles.

quiz.q: The vertebra with an odontoid process is the
quiz.solution: The odontoid peg of the axis fits into the atlas, allowing the head to rotate.

quiz.q: The elbow is an example of a
quiz.solution: A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only, like a door hinge.

quiz.q: Muscles that work in opposition to each other are described as
quiz.solution: When one of the pair contracts the other relaxes, e.g. biceps and triceps.
